lessons.title: Particles, states of matter and diffusion
lessons.programRef: Form 3 Chemistry — Particles, elements, compounds and mixtures (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the particle model of solids, liquids and gases.
Explain diffusion and Brownian motion as evidence for moving particles.
Explain changes of state in terms of particles.
reviewNotes: In the ammonia/hydrogen chloride demonstration the ring forms nearer the HCl end; the relative speeds depend on the relative masses (NH₃ 17, HCl 36.5). Check whether the syllabus asks for 'rates of diffusion' in Form 3 and note safety (fume cupboard).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: The particle model
blocks.md: All matter is made of tiny **particles** (atoms, molecules or ions) that are always **moving**. **Solid**: particles close together in a regular pattern, vibrating about fixed positions. **Liquid**: close together but able to slide past each other. **Gas**: far apart and moving fast in all directions, so gases fill their container and can be **compressed**. Heating makes particles move faster.

blocks.title: Evidence for particles
blocks.md: **Diffusion** is the spreading of particles from a region of high concentration to one of low concentration. A purple crystal of potassium manganate(VII) slowly colours the whole of the water, and the smell of cooking spreads through a house. **Brownian motion** is the random jiggling of tiny smoke or pollen grains seen under a microscope: it is caused by unseen, fast-moving air or water particles hitting them. Gases diffuse faster than liquids; **lighter** gas particles diffuse faster; diffusion is faster when **hot**.

items.text: The ring forms nearer the HCl end: ammonia particles are lighter and diffuse faster.

blocks.caption: Ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases diffusing along a tube.
blocks.alt: A glass tube with cotton wool soaked in ammonia at the left end and hydrochloric acid at the right end, and a white ring forming closer to the right end.

blocks.title: Changes of state
blocks.md: **Melting**: the particles vibrate more and break out of their pattern. **Boiling**: particles escape from the whole liquid. **Condensation**: slowing gas particles join together. During a change of state the temperature stays constant while energy breaks or forms the forces between particles. **Sublimation** (iodine, ammonium chloride): solid to gas without a liquid.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Particles do not get bigger when a solid melts: they stay the same size; only their arrangement and movement change.
- There is no air between the particles: the space between gas particles is empty.
- Diffusion does not need heating; heating only makes it faster.

blocks.title: State at room temperature
blocks.statement: Mercury melts at −39 °C and boils at 357 °C. Sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. State each at 25 °C.
steps: 25 °C lies between −39 °C and 357 °C, so mercury is a liquid.
25 °C is below 801 °C, so sodium chloride is a solid.

blocks.title: Explain a smell
blocks.statement: Explain why the smell of fried plantain reaches the next room.
steps: Particles of the vapour move randomly and fast in all directions.
They diffuse through the air from the kitchen to the room.

objectives: Define element, compound and mixture and give the symbols of the first 20 elements.
Compare the properties of metals and non-metals.
Distinguish compounds from mixtures and name alloys.
reviewNotes: The number of known elements (118) is the current figure; check the syllabus list of elements (first 20 plus some others such as Fe, Cu, Zn).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Elements, compounds, mixtures
blocks.md: An **element** has only one kind of atom and cannot be broken down by chemical means; there are about 118 known. A **compound** has atoms of **two or more elements chemically combined** in a fixed ratio, with properties different from the elements (sodium, a reactive metal, and chlorine, a poisonous gas, form harmless table salt). A **mixture** has substances only **physically mixed** in any proportion; each keeps its own properties and they can be separated.

blocks.caption: The first 20 elements: symbol and atomic number.
blocks.alt: A grid of 20 boxes from H 1 to Ca 20 giving each symbol and atomic number.

blocks.title: Metals and non-metals
blocks.md: **Metals** are shiny, **malleable**, **ductile**, good conductors of heat and electricity, usually solid with high melting points (mercury is liquid) and sonorous. **Non-metals** are dull, brittle if solid, poor conductors (graphite is an exception) and have lower melting points. An **alloy** is a mixture of a metal with another element: **brass** (copper and zinc), **bronze** (copper and tin), **steel** (iron and a little carbon). Alloys are often harder or less likely to rust.

blocks.title: Naming compounds
blocks.md: A compound of two elements ends in **-ide** (sodium chloride, magnesium oxide, iron sulphide). Compounds with oxygen as well end in **-ate** or **-ite** (copper sulphate, calcium carbonate, sodium nitrate). Formulae show the atoms: H₂O has two H and one O; CaCO₃ has one Ca, one C and three O.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Air is a mixture, not a compound: the gases in it are not chemically joined.
- Heating iron and sulphur makes a compound; mixing them only makes a mixture.
- A mixture can have any proportions; a compound always has a fixed one.

blocks.title: Classify
blocks.statement: Classify each as element, compound or mixture: oxygen, sea water, carbon dioxide, copper.
steps: Oxygen and copper each contain only one kind of atom: elements.
Carbon dioxide has C and O joined: compound. Sea water has water and salts: mixture.
blocks.answer: Elements: oxygen, copper. Compound: carbon dioxide. Mixture: sea water.

blocks.title: Count atoms and elements
blocks.statement: How many different elements and how many atoms are in one unit of Al₂(SO₄)₃?
steps: Elements: Al, S, O = 3 different elements.
